title: Why Empordà tastes the way it does

lede.text: A cold, dry wind from the north often gusts at over 120 km/h across Empordà's vineyards. It keeps the grapes healthy until harvest, and it shaped which varieties grow here.

chapters.title: The far north-east corner of Catalonia
paras: Empordà sits in the far north-east of Catalonia. The production zone takes in 55 municipalities in two separate areas: 35 in the Alt Empordà and 20 in the Baix Empordà.

The Alt Empordà is tucked below the Rodes and Alberes ranges, in an arc from Cap de Creus to the Garrotxa d'Empordà. The Pyrenees close it in to the north. The Mediterranean lies to the east, and the plain opens to the south.
The Baix Empordà is bounded by the Montgrí massif in the north and the Gavarres massif in the south-west. The sea is to the east. The Pyrenees reach close to 1500 m, while the Gavarres peak at 535 m.
Vines grow from sea level up to a maximum of 260 m.

chapters.title: The wind that shaped the vineyards
paras: The climate is Mediterranean, with about 600 mm of rain a year and an annual mean of 14 to 16 °C. Winters are mild with few frosts. Summers are hot but softened by sea breezes.

The Tramuntana is the most characteristic feature of the climate. This cold, dry north wind neutralises the excess damp that can build up now and then in the wettest seasons. That keeps disease away, so the grapes stay healthy right up to harvest.

Growers adapted to it long ago by choosing varieties with sturdier stems, such as Garnacha and Cariñena in their white, red and pink forms. They still dominate the vineyards today. On the plain, tall cypress trees, many of them centuries old, stand along the northern edge of fields as windbreaks. They bring a biodiversity that touches the primary aromas of the wines, with herbal and balsamic notes. In the coastal hills, dry-stone terraces show how the Tramuntana has set the lie of the vineyards for centuries. They already appear on the Cassini map of 1747.

Near the coast the sea tempers winter cold and keeps summer heat from spiking. This brings slow ripening, which gives the wines a distinctive elegance. Further inland the sea matters less, and the gap between day and night temperatures builds polyphenols and aroma compounds in the grapes. The wines there have deep colour and character, with high ageing potential.
On the Winkler scale the area falls in region III. That suits medium and long-cycle varieties and makes it outstanding for natural sweet wines.

fly.caption: The Tramuntana strongly marks the vineyards of Empordà. On the plain, cypress windbreaks line the northern edge of fields.

chapters.title: Many soils in a small space
paras: Few places pack so many soil types into so small an area. Most vines grow on poor, light soils that drain well and are acid to neutral. Most of the ground is sandy and low in organic matter.

In the mountains and mountain plateaus, granite and sandy soils sit beside slate soils, with a few pockets of limestone. Wines from granite and from the gently sloping gravel-and-clay ground show great tension and acidity, with moderate polyphenols.

Wines from slate and schist are different. They are high in alcohol and structured, with high polyphenol intensity. Most become long-aged reds that taste mineral and spicy, or long-lived whites of medium strength that are rich on the palate. The same ground also gives liqueur wines from slightly overripe grapes, such as Garnacha and Moscatel del Empordà.

On the plain, soils are mostly alluvial: marl and clay in places, conglomerate and sandstone in others. Still wines from there are light, balsamic and silky. They make excellent young whites, rosados (rosés) and reds that are fruity and fresh, with balanced acidity.
Producers know each kind of ground and have learned to complement their wines with grapes from parcels on different soils.

chapters.title: From fresh whites to century-old soleras
paras: Garnacha has a local name here. Lledoner negre is Garnacha Tinta, and Lledoner roig is a reddish Garnacha of Empordà. The recommended grapes are Garnacha and Cariñena in their white, red and black forms, with Macabeo and Moscatel de Alejandría. A long list of other grapes is authorised, among them Syrah, Merlot, Monastrell, Chardonnay and Picapoll Blanco.

The range is wide. There are whites and rosados, some fermented or aged in oak, and reds. A white called brisado is fermented with all its skins, pulp and pips, and sometimes the stalks, at least until fermentation ends. Needle wines (vinos de aguja) are lightly fizzy, with 1 to 2.5 bar of pressure. Sparkling wines are made by the traditional method and spend at least 9 months on their lees in the same bottle where the second fermentation happened.

Liqueur wines and wines from overripe grapes are deeply rooted here. The liqueur wines are fortified with wine spirit. Garnacha del Empordà is a liqueur wine from overripe grapes of at least 90% Garnacha, with 15 to 20% alcohol. It is called Ámbar when made from white or red Garnacha, and Rubí when made from Garnacha Tinta. It is usually aged in soleras, and some soleras are more than a century old.

Moscatel del Empordà comes from at least 90% Moscatel grapes, its fermentation stopped with wine spirit. Garnacha and Moscatel del Empordà may carry the words vino dulce natural when the must is very rich in sugar. Mistelas are made white or black with wine spirit. Vino dulce del Empordà is partly fermented and then fortified. Wines from overripe grapes (vino de uvas sobremaduradas) come from grapes left to overripen until they reach at least 18% natural alcohol. Rancio is made by oxidative ageing for at least 2 years.

The Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere de Rodes was founded on Cap de Creus at the end of the 9th century. It promoted vines along the coast. A record kept by its cellar monk in 1420 lists vineyards on Cap de Creus, with the Moscatel vines ranked as the most prized. In 1779 the Baron de Bourgoing described the local sweet wine as halfway between Jerez and Frontignan.

fly.caption: The Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere de Rodes promoted vines on this coast and prized its Moscatel in 1420.

terms.text: A wine sold with only its harvest year on the label, bottled in the harvest year or from 20 December of that year.
A wine aged for at least 12 months in oak barrels.
For reds, at least 24 months of ageing with at least 6 months in oak. For whites and rosados, at least 18 months with at least 6 months in oak.
